thinking_and_logic: The submitted implementation does not contain a real algorithm for Two Sum; it iterates but performs no checks and always returns [0, 1]. A correct approach per the answer key is either (1) brute force nested loops to check all pairs, or (2) the optimal single-pass hash map: for each number x at index i, compute complement = target - x; if complement has been seen, return [seen[complement], i]; otherwise store seen[x] = i. This avoids using the same element twice by only matching against previously seen indices.
code_assessment: Compared to the canonical optimal solution (single-pass hash map), the final code is missing the key technique entirely: tracking seen values and checking complements. As a result, it cannot adapt to different inputs and fails on basic placement changes (pair at end), sign variations (negative numbers), and differing expected index order (two elements). The hardcoded return matches a known pitfall in the answer key (hardcoding visible examples) and prevents correctness and robustness.

next_steps.action: Implement the optimal single-pass hash map Two Sum solution from scratch (no placeholders).
next_steps.why: It is the expected canonical approach: O(n) time, handles all placements and negatives, and prevents using the same element twice.
next_steps.how: Write: seen = {}; for i,x in enumerate(nums): c = target-x; if c in seen: return [seen[c], i]; seen[x]=i; return []
